extracted.intended_audience: aspiring satirists, humour-writers, periodical essayists and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing humour and satire in periodical essays and theatrical representation: how to distinguish true humour from false, choose proper targets, and keep tone, structure, and moral purpose appropriate for a broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour must be governed by reason and regularity of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour 'should always lye under the Check of Reason', and 'requires the Direction of the nicest Judgment' — there is a 'certain Regularity of Thought' in humour as in other compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the comic material is controlled by coherent thinking and structure; avoid indulgence in boundless caprice and delirious, incoherent conceits that read as madness rather than wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: True humour is descended from Truth and Good Sense (wit + mirth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addison's allegory: TRUTH → GOOD SENSE → WIT (married to MIRTH) → HUMOUR. True Humour is therefore lineally allied to Truth and Good Sense and is a mixture of wit and mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for humour that springs from accurate observation and sound judgment; combine cleverness (wit) with playfulness (mirth) so the piece enlightens as well as entertains.

rubrics_metrics.name: True humour often looks serious while others laugh (tone distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘TRUE HUMOUR generally looks serious, whilst every Body laughs; FALSE HUMOUR is always laughing, whilst every Body about him looks serious.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a restrained or serious surface tone that lets the audience perceive the joke; avoid noisy, self-congratulatory laughter in the text which signals spurious humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of False Humour (anti-pattern checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: False Humour differs from True as a 'Monkey does from a Man' and is marked by several faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for these defects — (1) excessive apish tricks and buffooneries; (2) overreliance on mimicry that indiscriminately exposes virtue as well as vice; (3) unlucky ridicule that bites friends and foes alike; (4) being void of reason and pursuing no moral or instructive point; (5) ridicule that is always personal (aimed at the man or writer) rather than the vice or the writing. Any of these indicate counterfeit humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid nonsense, frenzy, and monstrous conceits presented as humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers mistake incoherent, extravagant fancies and 'monstrous Conceits' for humour; speaking nonsense does not make a piece witty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on wild irregular fancies or delirious mirth; humour must remain intelligible and connected to human truth — otherwise readers will pity, not laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should attack vices and follies, not private persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer should 'assault the Vice without hurting the Person' and aim ridicule at the vice, not the vicious man or the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct criticism at the bad behaviour, affectation, or writing, not at the individual’s private reputation; keep moral focus rather than personal spite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer attacking multitudes/types over singling out individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator promises never 'to draw a faulty Character which does not fit at least a Thousand People' and will 'scourge Vice and Folly as they appear in a Multitude, without condescending to be a Publisher of particular Intrigues and Cuckoldoms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters and satirical targets representative (types) so readers of many ranks recognise the fault; avoid thinly veiled portraits of single private persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose public-useful targets (vanity, luxury, stage affectation) rather than trivial private scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate in the Club concludes the writer 'ought to employ [his] Pen upon the Vanity and Luxury of Courts' and to reprehend vices 'too trivial for the Chastisement of the Law, and too fantastical for the Cognizance of the Pulpit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus satire on social fashions, public affectations, institutional follies and the stage — matters of general consequence and instruction — rather than petty private scandals or municipal targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a spirit of benevolence and love of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper promises to be 'written in the Spirit of Benevolence and with a Love to Mankind' and to 'combat the Vice...without hurting the Person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a humane, corrective aim: satire should reform or expose for public good rather than vindictively shame; tone should be corrective rather than malicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: The periodical's role: correct minor vices beyond law or pulpit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator sees use 'in reprehending those Vices which are too trivial for the Chastisement of the Law, and too fantastical for the Cognizance of the Pulpit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the essay to illuminate and moderate everyday moral failings and fashionable follies that formal institutions cannot effectively address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should represent human affectation, not monsters or grossness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Drury-Lane petition says they will 'show no Monsters, but Men who are converted into such by their own Industry and Affectation' and will 'endeavour at these Regulations' to exclude gross monsters from the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing, prefer exposing social affectations and artificial manners rather than relying on grotesque, sensational monsters; satire on the stage should reveal affectation among the polite and well-bred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make content inclusive of social ranks (representative cast)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Club’s makeup assures the writer 'is furnished with the greatest Variety of Hints' and that readers 'have the Satisfaction to find, that there is no Rank or Degree among them who have not their Representative in this Club.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include examples and characters drawn from multiple social quarters so readers across classes see themselves represented and the satire feels widely relevant.
